This letter is in response to the â€œInteroperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for

These beneficiaries â€“ a large proportion of whom depend upon the MA program as their safety net â€“

We appreciate CMS' efforts to modernize, improve, and streamline prior authorization processes for 
providers, patients, and payers and support many of the provisions of the proposed rule. While we have 
provided more detailed comments below, we wanted to briefly share two of our key recommendations. 
 
Summary of Humanaâ€™s Key Issues and Recommendations 
 
â€¢ 
Humana encourages CMS to reconsider the proposed October 1, 2027, timeline for initial 
compliance. Based on impacted payersâ€™ experiences working internally and with vendors to 
implement requirements for the CMS-0057 final rule for medical items and services, we believe 
additional time will be needed beyond the proposed initial compliance date. Accordingly, we 
strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the Prior Authorization 
API and NCPDP standards for drugs until October 1, 2028. 
â€¢ 
Humana supports greater transparency for prior authorization decisions on medical benefit 
drugs. Humana remains committed to greater transparency on prior authorization. CMS has 
previously taken steps to require impacted payers to report standard metrics on prior 
authorization decisions for medical items and services. We recognize the value of extending such 
efforts to drugs covered under Medicare Part B and the Medicaid and CHIP programs.  
 
We hope that you consider our comments as constructive feedback aimed at ensuring that together we

If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to reach out to me at mhoak@humana.com and

Michael Hoak 
Vice President, Public Policy

II.A. Interoperability Standards for APIs 
Section II.A.2. National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) Standards for Prior 
Authorization of Drugs Covered Under a Pharmacy Benefit 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization for drugs, using 
either the FHIR standards and IGs required for the Prior Authorization API or the NCPDP SCRIPT standard 
depending upon whether the drugs are covered under a medical benefit or a pharmacy benefit, as 
detailed by the standards implementation specifications.  
 
Humana Comment: Humana is supportive of CMSâ€™ proposal to require use of the FHIR standards 
or the NCPDP standards, as appropriate, by impacted payers. This proposal essentially aligns 
requirements for impacted payers with those previously established for medical items and 
services and the Medicare Part D program. Greater standardization across programs and payers 
may improve the patient experience and ultimately streamline the prior authorization process. 
 
Although we support adoption of the proposed standards, the size and scope of these proposals 
are substantial, impacting a large and varied range of transactions, and will necessitate 
significant resources to implement. Humana is actively working towards compliance with the 
adopted API standards as they apply to Medicare Advantage and Medicare Part D plan sponsors, 
but those implementation dates also fall primarily during calendar year 2027. Impacted payers 
were given 2 full calendar years to implement the medical services and Part D standards, so 
extending the requirements to additional markets and services by October 1, 2027, seems 
extremely ambitious. We are concerned about the cumulative impact of these changes on 
impacted payers and their contracted vendors who assist in claims processing activities. 
Accordingly, we strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the Prior 
Authorization API and NCPDP standards under this rule until October 1, 2028. Humana also 
encourages CMS to take into account delegation arrangements with providers and other vendors 
for prior authorization functions when considering final policies and implementation timelines. 
 
In response to the questions regarding NCPDP Formulary & Benefit (F&B) files, Humana 
publishes our F&B files to eRx network intermediaries on a monthly basis. Formulary and benefit 
changes (including changes to prior authorization requirements) would be incorporated into the 
next monthly file. Humana believes the current cadence of updates is appropriate based on file 
utilization.  
 
CMS is proposing to require each impacted payer to implement and maintain APIs that are conformant 
with applicable standards in 45 CFR 170.215 in a manner that will allow for progressive adoption of new 
versions of these required standards. 
 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the proposal for impacted payers to implement and 
maintain APIs that are conformant with applicable standards in 45 CFR 170.215. 
 
Section II.A.5. Recommended Implementation Guides To Support Interoperability APIs and Request for 
Comment 
For the Provider Access API, CMS is recommending the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Member Attribution (ATR) List 
IG (ATR List IG). The ATR List IG provides specific technical guidance for payers and providers to exchange 
Member Attribution Lists. For the Prior Authorization API, CMS recommends the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci 
Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) IG. 
 
4 
 
Humana Comment: Humana supports CMSâ€™s recommendation of the ATR List IG. We believe 
implementation of Member Attribution (ATR) will streamline processes to share data for 
attributed membership via the Provider Access API. Similarly, Humana supports CMSâ€™s 
recommendation that impacted payers use the HL7 FHIR Da Vinci Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) 
IG for exchanging attachments related to prior authorization for the Prior Authorization API. 
 
Humana supports CMSâ€™s proposal to recommend the FAST Security IG â€œTiered OAuthâ€ in future 
rulemaking to support user authentication. We believe this IG should apply to the Provider 
Access API and the Payer-to-Payer API.  
 
Humana currently is not aware of trust communities that exist today that impacted payers could 
utilize for business-to-business authentication and authorization.  
 
Section II.A.6. Clarification of Standards for the Provider Directory FHIR API 
CMS is proposing that impacted payers be required to implement and maintain a Provider Directory API 
conformant with FHIR and US Core IG, but not the SMART App Launch IG or OpenID Connect Core. 
Humana Comment: Humana agrees with this approach. Humana already shares provider 
directory via FHIR server. We agree it should not be required via SMART App launch or Open ID 
connect. FHIR provides scalable approach to share provider directory data.  
 
Section II.B. Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Section II.B.3. Proposed Requirement To Incorporate Drugs Covered Under a Medical Benefit Into the 
Prior Authorization API for All Impacted Payers 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to expand the scope of the required Prior Authorization API to 
incorporate drugs covered under a medical benefit. CMS proposes an October 1, 2027, compliance date 
for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP 
managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports extension of the Prior Authorization API to include drugs 
covered under a medical benefit. As reflected throughout our comments, however, the 
application of these standards across impacted payers will require significant resources and 
planning. Many of these same payers are currently in the process of executing operational 
changes necessary for implementation of the Prior Authorization API for medical services, as 
well as full adoption of NCPDP formulary and real-time benefit standards in the Medicare Part D 
space. We remain concerned about the cumulative impact of these changes on impacted payers 
and their contracted vendors who assist in claims processing activities. Accordingly, we strongly 
recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the use of the Prior Authorization 
API for medical benefit drugs until October 1, 2028. Doing so would allow impacted payers to 
both ensure responsible resource allocation and apply any early learning from initiation of the 
Prior Authorization API for medical services on January 1, 2027. 
 
 
 
 
5 
 
Section II.B.4. Proposed Requirement To Support the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard for Prior Authorization for 
State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care 
Entities, and Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
CMS proposes to require state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP 
managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs to support an unexpired version of the NCPDP 
SCRIPT standard adopted by the Secretary in 45 CFR 170.205(b) for the electronic prior authorization of 
drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, as that term is described in the standard. CMS proposes an 
October 1, 2027, compliance date for state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care 
plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs. 
 
Humana Comment: Humana supports use of the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard by impacted payers. 
However, the application of this standard across impacted payers will require significant 
resources and planning. Many of these same payers are currently in the process of executing 
operational changes necessary for implementation of the SCRIPT standards in the Medicare Part 
D space. We remain concerned about the cumulative impact of these changes on impacted 
payers and their contracted vendors who assist with interoperability capabilities. Accordingly, we 
strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the use of the Prior 
Authorization API for medical benefit drugs until October 1, 2028. 
 
Section II.B.5. Proposed Requirement To Support the NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard for State 
Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care 
Entities, and Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
CMS proposes to require state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP 
managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs to support an unexpired version of the NCPDP F&B 
standard adopted by the Secretary in 45 CFR 170.205(u) by October 1, 2027. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports use of the NCPDP Formulary & Benefits (F&B) Standard 
by impacted payers. However, the application of this standard across impacted payers will 
require significant resources and planning. Many of these same payers are currently in the 
process of executing operational changes necessary for implementation of the F&B standards in 
the Medicare Part D space. We remain concerned about the cumulative impact of these changes 
on impacted payers and their contracted vendors who assist with interoperability capabilities. 
Accordingly, we strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the use 
of the Prior Authorization API for medical benefit drugs until October 1, 2028.  
 
Section II.B.6. Proposed Requirement To Support the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard for 
State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care 
Entities, and Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
CMS proposes that state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed 
care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs support an unexpired version of the NCPDP RTPB standard 
adopted by the Secretary in 45 CFR 170.205(c) by October 1, 2027. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports use of the NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) 
Standard by impacted payers. However, the application of this standard across impacted payers 
will require significant resources and planning. Many of these same payers are currently in the 
process of executing operational changes necessary for implementation of the RTPB standards in 
 
6 
 
the Medicare Part D space. We remain concerned about the cumulative impact of these changes 
on impacted payers and their contracted vendors who assist with interoperability capabilities. 
Accordingly, we strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the use 
of the Prior Authorization API for medical benefit drugs until October 1, 2028. 
 
Section II.C. Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes for Prior Authorizations 
Section II.C.2.c. Proposed Requirement To Include a Specific Reason for Denial to Providers When 
Denying Prior Authorization of All Drugs for State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid 
Managed Care Plans, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Qualified Health Plan Issuers on the Federally-
facilitated Exchanges 
CMS proposes that beginning October 1, 2027, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid 
managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs be required to provide a 
specific reason to providers when denying a prior authorization request for drugs, regardless of the 
method used to send the prior authorization request or decision. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the CMS proposal to require state Medicaid and CHIP FFS 
programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the 
FFEs to provide a specific reason to providers when denying a prior authorization request for 
drugs, regardless of the method used to send the prior authorization request or decision, 
beginning October 1, 2027. This requirement is aligned with broader efforts to improve the 
transparency of the prior authorization process, which Humana supports.  
 
Humana already provides specific reasons for denials for drugs as part of our Medicaid managed 
care plans, per many state requirements. If CMS moves forward with this requirement, we 
encourage CMS to provide for consistent rules around the reason submissions, as appropriate.  
 
Section II.C.3.c. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes for Drugs That Are Not Covered Outpatient 
Drugs for State Medicaid Fee-for-Service Programs, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, and CHIP Managed 
Care Entities 
CMS seeks input on whether there are gaps in the decision timeframe requirements for drugs. If there 
are, CMS proposes to apply the same requirements to Medicaid MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs by amending 
42 CFR 438.210 and CHIP managed care entities by the existing cross reference to 42 CFR 438.210 in 42 
CFR 457.1230(d). CMS proposes an October 1, 2027, compliance date. 
Humana Comment: Humana is supportive of the CMS proposal to align the prior authorization 
decision timeframe for a drug that meets the limiting definition in section 1927(k)(3) of the Act 
(or is not a covered outpatient drug) with the services it is provided as part of, or incident to. 
This timeline, which is 7 calendar days for standard requests and 72 hours for expedited 
requests, is a more appropriate standard for more complex drug therapies, such as gene 
therapies, which often require detailed review and planning for administration. A 24-hour review 
standard for these drugs would therefore not be necessary or practical. Additionally, Humana 
believes the CMS proposal appropriately provides for adequate clinical review to identify any 
potential safety concerns or other factors to ensure appropriate use of these treatments. 
 
While we consider the proposed timelines appropriate, we also note that many providers 
continue to submit prior authorization requests via phone or fax. Moving forward, we support 
 
7 
 
efforts to encourage providers to utilize electronic prior authorization requests to maximize the 
potential efficiencies associated with electronic prior authorization standards.    
 
CMS also seeks feedback on whether the agency should consider future rulemaking to propose a 
requirement for MA organizations to respond to all prior authorization requests for drugs no later than 
24 hours to align with the Medicaid and CHIP requirements for covered outpatient drugs.  
Humana Comment: We generally believe the MA organization requirement allowing for a 24-
hour expedited prior authorization request is appropriate to ensure timely access for our 
members. Prior authorization builds necessary checks and balances into the healthcare system 
by verifying that a requested medication is medically necessary. We believe that current 
standards allow for prior authorization processes that reduce unnecessary care and ensure high-
quality, cost-effective care, but would welcome dialogue with CMS around situations where a 
change to this requirement would be necessary.    
 
CMS requests input on whether there are any drugs payable under Medicare Part A that are not included 
as part of a larger bundle of inpatient services to which the timeframe to make prior authorizations 
decisions should apply for MA organizations. 
Humana Comment: Humana does not generally require separate prior authorization for drugs 
payable under Part A and provided as part of an inpatient visit, as these can be submitted under 
one authorization for the drug and accompanying services. 
 
Section II.C.5. Proposed Changes to Reporting Deadlines and Reporting Levels for Publicly Reported Prior 
Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items and Services for Medicaid Managed Care Plans and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities 
CMS proposes to require Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities to publicly post 
the required prior authorization metrics no later than 90 days after the end of their rating period. CMS 
also proposes to amend the existing requirements for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed 
care entities to require that they report the prior authorization metrics finalized in the 2024 CMS 
Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule by program, as well as by plan. For consistency with the 
other Medicaid and CHIP managed care reporting requirements, CMS believes that it is appropriate to 
also collect these metrics at the program level.  
Humana Comment: Humana supports CMSâ€™s proposal for Medicaid managed care plans and 
CHIP managed care entities to post the required prior authorization metrics no later than 90 
days after the end of their rating period. 
 
Section II.C.6. Proposed Changes to Publicly Reported Prior Authorization Metrics for Non-Drug Items 
and Services for Impacted Payers 
CMS proposes to modify existing requirements to publicly report prior authorization metrics for non-
drug items and services by requiring payers to report a numeric count of prior authorization requests, as 
well as percentages, for certain existing metrics. CMS also proposes to add four new metrics to be 
reported by impacted payers: The total number and percentage of standard prior authorization requests 
for non-drug items and services that remain denied after appeal during the reporting period; the total 
 
8 
 
number and percentage of expedited prior authorization requests for non-drug items and services that 
remain denied after appeal during the reporting period; the total number and percentage of standard 
prior authorization requests for non-drug items and services for which the timeframe for review was 
extended, and the request was denied during the reporting period; the total number and percentage of 
expedited prior authorization requests for non-drug items and services for which the timeframe for 
review was extended, and the request was denied during the reporting period. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the proposed update to prior authorization metrics for 
non-drug items and services. Humana remains committed to greater transparency on prior 
authorization. 
 
Section II.C.7. Proposed Requirement To Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics for Drugs for 
Impacted Payers 
CMS proposes that impacted payers, other than Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care 
entities, be required to annually report the previous calendar year's metrics regarding all drugs, 
excluding covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs, on their public websites beginning in 2028 (with data from 
2027) following any calendar year that any of these impacted payers offered that type of plan. We 
propose to require that these metrics be made publicly available on those impacted payers' websites no 
later than March 31. State Medicaid and Medicaid managed care plans would report on all prescribed 
drugs described in section 1905(a)(12) of the Act that require prior authorization.  
Humana Comment: Humana is committed to greater transparency on prior authorization and 
supports these proposals.   
 
In addition, CMS requests comments on whether there are drugs payable under Part A that require prior 
authorization separate from other non-drug items and services that should be included in the scope of 
the proposed metrics for MA organizations. 
Humana Comment: Humana does not generally require separate prior authorization for drugs 
payable under Part A and provided as part of an inpatient visit, as these can be submitted under 
one authorization for the drug and accompanying services. Therefore, we do not believe that 
additional reporting metrics should be required for drugs administered under those 
circumstances. 
 
Section II.E. Reporting Payer API Endpoints and Associated Information for CMS To Publish 
Section II.E.1. API Endpoints 
CMS is proposing to require impacted payers to report to CMS their API endpoints for each required 
interoperability API. To ensure the standardization of payer endpoints, we are proposing to require 
impacted payers to report their API endpoints as an Endpoint Resource, as defined by an unexpired 
version of the Health Level Seven (HL7Â®) FHIRÂ® standard adopted in 45 CFR 170.215(a). 
Humana Comment: Humana agrees with CMS that a payer digital endpoint directory would 
improve the ability of payers, providers, patients, and developers to use the interoperability 
APIs. We believe this could provide an opportunity to streamline data exchange by providing a 
central repository for interoperability API endpoints. To ease the burden that reporting API 
endpoints could place on payers, Humana encourages CMS to support a trustable national payer 
 
9 
 
directory with the appropriate URLs as a resource for impacted payers and other healthcare data 
stakeholders. 
 
Section II.E.4. Reporting Timeline 
As new payers participate in CMS programs, CMS proposes that they would be required to report the 
proposed information to CMS no later than 60 days before they begin covering patients under the 
applicable CMS program. After the proposed deadline, CMS proposes that impacted payers would be 
required to update the information reported to CMS within 1 week of any changes. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the proposed timeline for new payers to report the 
proposed information to CMS no later than 60 days before they begin covering patients under 
the applicable CMS program. Humana supports the proposal to require any changes to be 
reported to CMS within 1 week.    
 
Section II.F. Updates to Patient Access, Provider Directory, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs; 
API Usage Metrics 
Section II.F.1.b. Information About Prior Authorizations for Drugs in the Patient Access, Provider Access, 
and Payer-to-Payer APIs - Proposals  
Consistent with CMS policies for non-drug items and services, the information about prior authorizations 
for drugs that CMS is proposing be made available via the Patient Access and Provider Access APIs is the 
following:  
â€¢ 
The prior authorization status. 
â€¢ 
The date the prior authorization was approved or denied. 
â€¢ 
The date or circumstance under which the prior authorization ends. 
â€¢ 
The drug or drugs approved (including the dosage). 
â€¢ 
If denied, a specific reason why the request was denied. 
â€¢ 
Related structured administrative and clinical documentation submitted by a provider. 
For the Payer-to-Payer API, the information about prior authorizations for drugs CMS propose is the 
following: 
â€¢ 
The prior authorization status. 
â€¢ 
The date the prior authorization was approved. 
â€¢ 
The date or circumstance under which the prior authorization ends. 
â€¢ 
The drug or drugs approved (including the dosage). 
â€¢ 
Related structured and unstructured administrative and clinical documentation submitted by a 
provider. 
CMS proposes an October 1, 2027, compliance date for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS 
programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs to 
make the proposed information about prior authorizations for drugs available via the Access APIs.  
CMS proposes that the requirement to make available information about prior authorization for drugs 
would be subject to the same timeframes established for making available prior authorization 
information for non-drug items and servicesâ€”no later than 1 business day after the payer receives a 
 
10 
 
prior authorization requestâ€”and the payer must update that information no later than 1 business day 
after any status change. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the inclusion of the proposed data elements about prior 
authorizations for drugs in the Patient Access API, Provider Access API, and Payer-to-Payer API. 
As stated previously, Humana remains committed to greater transparency on prior authorization. 
However, we remain concerned about the cumulative impact of changes affecting drug prior 
authorizations on impacted payers and their contracted vendors who assist with interoperability 
capabilities. Accordingly, we strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date 
for inclusion of the proposed data elements about prior authorizations for drugs in the Patient 
Access API, Provider Access API, and Payer-to-Payer API until October 1, 2028. 
 
Section II.F.2.b. Proposed Changes to Patient Access API Usage Metrics for Medicaid Managed Care 
Plans, CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Individual Market QHP Issuers on the FFEs 
To simplify the cross-referencing regulatory text, CMS also proposes, in 42 CFR 438.242(b)(5)(ii)(B), to be 
explicit that the requirement for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities is to 
report API usage metrics to the state, rather than to CMS directly. CMS proposes to amend the 
requirements for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities to clarify that they 
would be required to report the Patient Access API usage metrics by program, as well as by plan. We 
plan to collect metrics from Medicaid managed care plans via the states through the MCPAR system, 
which is set up to receive reports from plans by program. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports CMSâ€™s proposal to clarify that Medicaid managed care 
and CHIP managed care entities would report API usage metrics to the state. Conversely, 
Humana encourages CMS to reconsider its proposal to report API utilization metrics at the 
program level for Medicaid managed care plans. Because Medicaid enrollees in many cases 
move among different programs throughout the year, breaking out utilization metrics by 
program could be less informative than data reported at the plan level. 
 
Section II.F.2.c. Proposal to Report Metrics About the Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior 
Authorization API Usage for All Impacted Payers 
CMS is proposing that impacted payers be required to report metrics about usage of the Provider Access, 
Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs. The reporting period for MA organizations, state Medicaid 
and CHIP FFS programs, and QHP issuers on the FFEs would be the calendar year, while the reporting 
period for Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP managed care entities would be the rating period. 
CMS proposes that, beginning in 2028, MA organizations and state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs be 
required to report the previous calendar year's metrics to CMS by March 31 of each year. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the reporting of utilization metrics to CMS for the 
Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs. We believe this data can help 
future CMS policymaking as an input to cost-benefit analyses of future rulemaking.  
 
 
 
 
11 
 
3.b. Removing Drug Formulary Information From the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs - Proposals 
CMS proposes to remove drug formulary information as data required to make available via the Provider 
Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs for MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid 
managed care plans, and CHIP managed care entities. If finalized, CMS proposes that this would be 
effective beginning on the effective date of the final rule. In addition, CMS requests comments on 
whether there are use cases where it would be helpful for any party to have access to drug formulary 
data via those APIs. 
Humana Comment: Humana supports CMSâ€™ intent to remove drug formulary information as a 
required data element in the Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs for impacted payers. CMS 
is correct in noting that MA organizations and Medicaid managed care plans furnish formulary 
information to providers and patients in a variety of ways.  Accordingly, we are inclined to agree 
that the formulary information which could be furnished through the APIs is redundant and 
unnecessary. CMS proposes to treat this data as an optional submission that may still be offered 
via the APIs in cases where a payer sees value in providing formulary information. Humana 
believes this approach strikes a reasonable balance between appropriate information sharing 
and administrative simplicity. 
 
Section III. Requests for Information 
A. Request for Information: Electronic Event Notifications for Value-Based Care and Care Coordination 
CMS requests input from providers on how to improve the availability and usability of electronic event 
notifications to support value-based care and care coordination. While CMS posed an array of questions, 
Humana focuses its response here on issues related to types of providers and entities receiving patient 
event notifications. 
Humana Comment: Humana believes that Patient Event Notifications are an important tool for 
value-based care entities, including accountable care organizations (ACOs) and payers. The 
CenterWell ACO â€“ part of Humanaâ€™s CenterWell primary care organization -- uses ADT event 
notifications to aid in post-discharge care coordination with preferred providers such as home 
health, and/or skilled nursing facilities.  An example of a specific workflow includes the ACO 
receiving ADT notifications from a state health information exchange (HIE). The ACO then routes 
the alerts to a preferred Home Health provider that can contact the ACO member to schedule a 
post-discharge home visit. 
 
Based on the value of Patient Event Notifications in care coordination efforts, Humana supports 
efforts by CMS to require hospitals to make ADT feeds available to eligible 
providers/suppliers. Humana takes the position that this information should not be subject to 
bias or used as bargaining leverage in contract negotiations.  Furthermore, patient event 
notifications should be more easily accessible. The fragmented nature of health information 
exchanges and private health aggregators can make things more complex and unwieldy.  A 
national event notification system may need to be considered to facilitate a consistent 
interoperability experience.  
 
In the context of patient attribution, Humana encourages CMS to consider opportunities to 
leverage new model designs, potentially including the CMS Adjudicated Risk Arrangements 
(CARA) under the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) model.  Humana believes CARA could 
provide a structure for parties to design incentives around episodes that would require flagging 
 
12 
 
or matching ACO patients in an acute setting.  This identification or matching process could lead 
to greater coordination and data sharing as parties work together to manage ACO patients 
against episode benchmarks.  However, where voluntary incentive structures do not drive 
results, Humana encourages CMS to consider penalties for facilities that continuously put up 
barriers to coordinating care or who restrict data exchange. 
 
C. Request for Information: Implementation of Payer Application Programming Interface Technology 
Roadmap for Consistent Implementation of Payer API Technology 
Among other questions, CMS requested input on the aspects of API implementation that pose the most 
significant implementation difficulties, as well which aspects of API implementation should be prioritized 
for testing. 
Humana Comment: Humana encourages CMS to pursue options to simplify information about 
interoperability requirements for APIs. Something as direct as a checklist or other resource that 
is focused on API capabilities would be very helpful to the payer community. Such a resource 
would be especially helpful to address challenges regarding versioning and the schedule for IG 
updates. In addition, a certification framework would be a helpful resource for impacted payers 
to validate that APIs developed internally or offered by vendors meet current requirements. 
With regard to API testing, Humana strongly encourages CMS to prioritize efforts related to 
identification and authentication. This will be especially important as utilization of the APIs 
increases and payers are managing significantly more data requests than ever before. In 
addition, Humana encourages CMS to consider supporting a common data repository to support 
industry testing of APIs.  
D. Request for Information: Step Therapy 
CMS solicits feedback on ways in which increased data interoperability could streamline step therapy 
processes for prescription drugs. CMS offers a range of queries on the use of information sharing 
technologies to improve the step therapy experience for payers, providers, and patients. CMS is 
particularly interested in using technology to reduce repetitive step therapy protocols and delays in care. 
CMS seeks input on the types of technical solutions that could facilitate fast, efficient, and accurate step 
therapy determinations moving forward.   
 
Humana Comment: Humana supports the concept of increased data interoperability for 
communicating step therapy requirements to providers and patients. Despite inclusion of this 
information in RTPB and formulary information posted by payers, accessing and understanding 
this information continues to be a challenge for providers. Today we see some providers submit 
appeals letters in excess of 10 pages long, which appear to be generated with support from AI 
solutions. Often times, these letters do not provide the data needed for payer approvals and can 
cause delays in processing appeals.  
 
Additional data interoperability may allow providers or plans to access and utilize data related to 
a patient intolerance or poor response to initial treatments, streamlining step therapy processes 
for patients, providers and payers and avoiding confusion about what information needs to be 
submitted for a payer to confirm a patient meets step therapy protocol requirements. Although 
increased information sharing through the Payer-to-Payer API could expedite plan approvals, this 
approach requires members to opt-in and has not yet been in effect for use with non-drug 
 
13 
 
medical services, so practical experience is limited. We suggest that CMS apply any learnings 
from the Payer-to-Payer API use for non-drug services to drugs where appropriate. Additionally, 
more widespread access to patient clinical histories or claims data could help payers avoid 
lengthy information exchanges with providers to gain information needed for step therapy 
processes. However, we would note that when a patient is stable on a medication, that stability 
is typically used to bypass any step therapy requirements or additional review to favor 
continuation of care.  
 
Although we support the provision of additional information to payers, we would be concerned 
about any proposal that might limit payer flexibility with regard to step therapy protocols. For 
example, in the Medicare Part B space, Humana generates savings for patients and the Medicare 
program by preferring generic and biosimilar medications over therapeutically equivalent 
branded products. We continue to see step therapy as a valuable tool in promoting biosimilar 
medications in the pharmaceutical pipeline and selectively use this tool to encourage use of 
lower-cost alternatives and/or clinically appropriate use by our members when appropriate.  
 
As the availability of, and real-world experience with, biosimilar medications continues to 
expand, we recommend that plans be afforded the flexibility to require step therapy for 
members receiving maintenance therapy, in addition to those initiating treatment, rather than 
limiting such requirements to new starts as is currently the case. 
 
Step Therapy by Previous Payer 
 
CMS solicits feedback on standard practices used by payers with respect to step therapy protocols 
completed by a patient under a previous payer. CMS recognizes that formularies and processes vary 
from payer to payer and seeks input on how these varied processes can be better aligned. CMS also 
seeks feedback on how payers can more effectively share information to limit the repetition of step 
therapy protocols to reduce the burden on payers, providers, and patients. 
 
Humana Comment: As suggested above, Humana supports CMS efforts to identify mechanisms 
that streamline step therapy processes for impacted payers, providers, and patients. The step 
therapy processes applied â€“ and the decisions made â€“ by a previous payer can be a valuable 
resource in making coverage determinations for the current plan year and looking forward. 
However, we believe that step therapy decisions from a previous payer should not be the 
primary metric for current coverage determinations.  
 
Evolving clinical standards and the consistent development of new medications, biosimilars, and 
generics dictates that impacted payers consistently refine their formularies and utilization 
management processes. Unlike discrete medical services, which are typically rendered at a single 
point in time, medications for chronic conditions are often used on a long-term or even lifelong 
basis. Over the course of such treatment, clinical guidelines regarding safety and efficacy may 
evolve. Periodic re-evaluation of therapy is therefore essential to ensure continued 
appropriateness. Allowing plans to reassess utilization management criteria supports the 
delivery of care that reflects the most current evidence, while also incorporating the 
beneficiaryâ€™s clinical experience and the prescribing physicianâ€™s ongoing oversight.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Humana Inc.; signed by Michael Hoak, Vice President, Public Policy.
- **Stakeholder type:** Payer
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Humana states it serves approximately 7.1 million Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, 3.8 million Medicare Part D PDP beneficiaries, and Medicaid beneficiaries in seven states.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Humana supports many of CMS's interoperability and drug prior authorization proposals, including use of FHIR and NCPDP standards, denial-reason transparency, public PA metrics, API endpoint reporting, and drug PA data in access APIs. Its primary modification request is to delay the October 1, 2027 compliance date to October 1, 2028 because of cumulative implementation demands on payers and vendors; it also asks CMS to preserve payer flexibility for complex drug review and step therapy while simplifying API implementation guidance.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.215; 45 CFR 170.205(b), (c), and (u); 42 CFR 438.210; 42 CFR 457.1230(d); section 1927(k)(3) of the Act; section 1905(a)(12) of the Act; 42 CFR 438.242(b)(5)(ii)(B).
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; US Core IG; SMART App Launch; OpenID Connect Core; HL7 Da Vinci Member Attribution (ATR) List IG; HL7 Da Vinci Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) IG; FAST Security IG Tiered OAuth; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit (F&B); NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB); Endpoint Resource.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: FHIR and NCPDP standards for drug PA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports standardization across programs and payers but says the proposals are substantial and overlap with 2027 implementation of CMS-0057 medical-services APIs and Part D NCPDP standards.
- **Specific request:** Adopt the standards but delay compliance for the Prior Authorization API and NCPDP drug standards until October 1, 2028, including medical benefit drugs, SCRIPT, F&B, RTPB, and drug PA data in access APIs.

**Topic 2: API standards, IGs, and provider directory approach**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports API conformance to 45 CFR 170.215, ATR for Provider Access, CDex for PA attachments, and FAST Security Tiered OAuth for future authentication. It also agrees the Provider Directory API should use FHIR and US Core without SMART App Launch or OpenID Connect.
- **Specific request:** Continue using applicable unexpired standards and recommended IGs, and apply FAST Security to Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs in future rulemaking.

**Topic 3: Pharmacy benefit standards and F&B cadence**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB requirements but cites resource burden and vendor impact. It reports that its F&B files are published monthly and that monthly updates are appropriate based on current utilization.
- **Specific request:** Delay compliance to October 1, 2028 and maintain the current monthly F&B update cadence.

**Topic 4: Specific denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Humana already provides specific denial reasons for drugs in Medicaid managed care under many state requirements and supports transparency.
- **Specific request:** Finalize the requirement but provide consistent rules around reason submissions where appropriate.

**Topic 5: Drug PA decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports aligning timeframes for drugs not meeting the covered outpatient drug framework with the service they are part of, citing complex therapies such as gene therapies that require clinical review and administration planning.
- **Specific request:** Use 7 calendar days for standard and 72 hours for expedited requests for those complex drugs; do not require all MA drug PA requests to be completed within 24 hours, though 24-hour expedited review is appropriate.

**Topic 6: Public PA metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY / GENERAL
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports public reporting of PA metrics for non-drug items/services and drugs, but notes it generally does not separately authorize Part A drugs provided as part of inpatient services.
- **Specific request:** Finalize metrics updates, post Medicaid managed care/CHIP metrics within 90 days after the rating period, and do not add separate Part A drug metrics where the drug and services are under one authorization.

**Topic 7: API endpoint reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana agrees a payer endpoint directory would improve use of interoperability APIs and supports the proposed 60-day pre-coverage and 1-week update timelines.
- **Specific request:** CMS should support a trustable national payer directory with appropriate URLs to reduce payer reporting burden.

**Topic 8: Drug PA data in Patient, Provider, and Payer-to-Payer APIs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports including drug PA status, dates, duration, dosage, denial reason, and documentation in access APIs, but repeats concerns about cumulative implementation demands.
- **Specific request:** Delay compliance for these data elements until October 1, 2028.

**Topic 9: API usage metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, Prior Authorization, and Patient Access API metrics as useful for future policymaking and cost-benefit analysis, but questions Medicaid program-level reporting because enrollees move between programs.
- **Specific request:** Medicaid managed care and CHIP plans should report to states, but CMS should reconsider program-level API utilization reporting and prioritize plan-level usefulness.

**Topic 10: Formulary data in access APIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Humana agrees formulary data in Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs is redundant because payers provide formulary information through other channels.
- **Specific request:** Remove formulary information as a required data element and allow optional submission where payers see value.

**Topic 11: RFIs on event notifications, API roadmap, and step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Humana supports ADT/event notifications for value-based care, wants simpler API implementation resources, and supports interoperability for step therapy while preserving payer flexibility for biosimilars, generics, and reassessment of maintenance therapy.
- **Specific request:** Consider a national event notification system; create API checklists, certification, authentication testing, and common testing data repositories; apply Payer-to-Payer API lessons to drugs; and allow step therapy flexibility including maintenance therapy where clinically appropriate.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1-S3:** Supports API conformance to adopted standards in 45 CFR 170.215 and progressive standards adoption, while requesting clearer versioning guidance.
- **S12:** Supports adding medical benefit drugs to the Prior Authorization API but asks CMS to delay compliance to October 1, 2028.
- **S14:** Supports NCPDP SCRIPT for pharmacy benefit drug PA for impacted payers, with a requested delay to October 1, 2028.
- **S19:** Raises state and plan implementation burden for Medicaid/CHIP and QHP pharmacy benefit drug standards.
- **S20:** Supports 7-day standard and 72-hour expedited timeframes for complex non-covered-outpatient drugs tied to broader services, and says a universal 24-hour MA drug timeframe is not necessary or practical.
- **S21:** Says the October 1, 2027 timeline is too ambitious and recommends October 1, 2028 for medical benefit drug PA API compliance.
- **S22:** Notes significant resource and vendor burden for implementing NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB across impacted payers.
- **S23-S24:** Supports endpoint reporting using FHIR Endpoint Resource and suggests a trusted national payer directory to reduce burden.
- **S25:** Supports RTPB standards but asks for delayed compliance because impacted payers are still implementing Part D requirements.
- **S26-S27:** Supports reporting new payer API information 60 days before coverage begins and updates within 1 week of changes.
- **S29-S30:** Supports API utilization metrics, including metrics for Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, and Prior Authorization APIs, as useful for future policy analysis.
- **S34-S35:** Supports annual public PA metrics and API metric reporting, while questioning Medicaid program-level breakouts.
- **S40-S42:** Supports applying requirements to QHP issuers on FFEs but includes them in the broader request for additional implementation time.
- **S60-S65:** Requests API capability checklists, clearer IG version schedules, certification, identity/authentication testing, and common testing data repositories.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on event notifications, API roadmap, and step therapy, supporting interoperability while preserving payer utilization-management flexibility.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Delay initial compliance for drug Prior Authorization API and NCPDP standards from October 1, 2027 to October 1, 2028.
2. Account for payer delegation arrangements with providers and vendors in implementation timelines.
3. Maintain monthly NCPDP F&B file updates.
4. Finalize support for FHIR/US Core provider directory without SMART App Launch or OpenID Connect requirements.
5. Support ATR, CDex, and future FAST Security Tiered OAuth guidance.
6. Finalize specific denial-reason requirements with consistent submission rules.
7. Keep complex drug PA timeframes at 7 calendar days standard and 72 hours expedited where clinical review and administration planning are needed.
8. Encourage providers to use electronic PA rather than phone or fax.
9. Finalize PA metrics for drugs and non-drugs but avoid unnecessary separate Part A drug metrics.
10. Create or support a trusted national payer endpoint directory.
11. Delay required drug PA data in Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs until October 1, 2028.
12. Reconsider Medicaid managed care program-level API usage reporting.
13. Remove formulary data as a required Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer API element.
14. Consider national event notification infrastructure and penalties for persistent data-exchange barriers.
15. Provide API checklists, certification, identity/authentication testing, and common testing data.
16. Preserve payer flexibility for step therapy, including biosimilars, generics, and maintenance therapy reassessment.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Compressed October 1, 2027 implementation timeline, cumulative burden from overlapping CMS-0057 and Part D work, vendor capacity, program-level reporting usefulness, identity/authentication readiness, and limits on payer step therapy flexibility.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Unmanageable implementation burden, less informative Medicaid metrics, delayed appeals if provider submissions lack necessary data, and reduced ability to promote lower-cost biosimilars or generics.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Vendor dependencies, claims-processing delegation, IG versioning, authentication and authorization, limited practical experience with Payer-to-Payer API for non-drug services, provider phone/fax submissions, and fragmented HIE/event notification infrastructure.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Humana serves approximately 7.1 million MA beneficiaries and 3.8 million PDP beneficiaries; Medicaid beneficiaries in seven states.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None cited.
- **Examples provided:** Monthly F&B files to eRx intermediaries; gene therapies requiring detailed review; Part A inpatient drugs typically under one authorization; CenterWell ACO use of ADT notifications; AI-generated appeals letters exceeding 10 pages that may lack needed approval data.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** MA organizations, PDPs, Medicaid/CHIP managed care plans, state Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHP issuers, contracted vendors, providers, patients, developers, ACOs, and CMS.
- **Economic implications:** Delayed compliance may reduce implementation strain and vendor costs; preserving step therapy can support lower-cost biosimilars and generics; API metrics can support future cost-benefit analysis.
- **Technical feasibility:** Humana supports the technical direction but says versioning, authentication, certification, testing, endpoint discovery, and overlapping deployments need more time and structure.
- **Patient care impact:** Better APIs, endpoint directories, metrics, event notifications, and drug PA data can improve transparency and coordination; overly compressed or overly restrictive requirements could compromise review quality or plan flexibility.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, and implementation-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "we strongly recommend that CMS delay the proposed compliance date for the Prior Authorization API and NCPDP standards for drugs until October 1, 2028." - Context: Humana's primary recommendation.
2. "Humana is supportive of CMS' proposal to require use of the FHIR standards or the NCPDP standards" - Context: Support for the core standards approach.
3. "Humana supports the CMS proposal... to provide a specific reason to providers when denying a prior authorization request for drugs" - Context: Support for denial-reason transparency.
4. "a certification framework would be a helpful resource for impacted payers" - Context: API roadmap recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Humana repeatedly requests delaying the October 1, 2027 compliance date to October 1, 2028.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - The comment emphasizes significant resources, vendor burden, and cumulative implementation costs.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Humana supports electronic PA adoption and notes provider phone/fax submissions and lengthy appeals letters can slow processing.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - It prioritizes identification and authentication testing and supports FAST Security Tiered OAuth.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Technical feasibility concerns include versioning, testing, certification, endpoint directories, and API readiness.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Humana discusses unexpired standards, 45 CFR 170.215, IG update schedules, and certification needs.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Supports transparency and access APIs but argues complex drug reviews require sufficient time for safety and appropriateness.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment highlights payer, provider, vendor, HIE, ACO, and CMS coordination needs.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports denial reasons, public PA metrics, endpoint directories, and drug PA data in APIs.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Requests alignment with delegated arrangements, existing F&B monthly processes, provider submission patterns, and care coordination workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Humana repeatedly cites contracted vendors and the need for certification/testing support.
